diligent

DIL-ih-jent -- stress on the first syllable, DIL. · adjective

What It Means

Diligent is marked by steady, earnest, and careful effort.

The diligent apprentice checked every measurement twice before cutting a single board.

Example

Night after night, the diligent student reviews her notes, redoes the problems she missed, and updates her study plan -- long after her classmates have logged off.

That steady, careful, earnest effort, kept up consistently over time, is what it means to be diligent. Unlike a burst of last-minute cramming, diligence is patient work done thoroughly and without shortcuts.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

industrious: Industrious praises how consistently busy and productive someone is — always making, doing, producing more. Diligent shifts the spotlight from the amount produced to the quality of the effort: steady, careful, earnest work done without shortcuts, the kind that gets every detail right.

painstaking: Painstaking describes the work itself — done with such great care that every detail costs real effort, like a painstaking restoration of an old map. Diligent describes the worker's steady habit: careful, earnest effort kept up day after day, not lavished on one exacting task.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

lazy: unwilling to work or make an effort

negligent: careless; failing to take proper care

Where it sits · how careful and constant the effort is — hardworking → diligent → assiduous

hardworking vs. diligent: Hardworking is the plainer, broader word -- it praises the amount of effort, while diligent adds care and steadiness: a diligent worker is not just busy but careful, thorough, and consistent.

assiduous vs. diligent: Assiduous turns the intensity up a notch beyond diligent: both describe careful, persistent effort, but assiduous suggests almost tireless, meticulous attention that never lets up even in the smallest details.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — di-

Prefix — di-: apart (a form of Latin dis-)

Root — lig

Root — lig: to choose, to gather (from Latin legere -- the same root spelled lig- in eligible and leg- in select's cousin elegant)

Suffix — -ent

Suffix — -ent: adjective-forming: doing or being (Latin -ens, -entis)

Put it together

Put it together: Di- ('apart') + lig ('to choose', from Latin legere) + -ent (adjective ending) spell diligent. Latin diligere meant 'to single out, to value highly' -- a diligent person, at the root, is one who has chosen their task apart from everything else and gives it their full, loving attention.

Use the root in a new word: eligible

Use the root in a new word: eligible: Students with at least a B average are eligible for the honors program.

Word Choice

Diligent praises quality of effort, not just quantity -- steady, careful, earnest work. It pairs naturally with roles and habits: a diligent student, diligent practice, a diligent search. It is one of the core words of the determination-and-effort family.
